questions.stem: Ice floats on liquid water. Which property of water explains this?
options: Ice is less dense than liquid water
Ice is denser than liquid water
Ice has a higher boiling point
Ice has a lower surface tension
questions.explanation: When water freezes, hydrogen bonds hold the molecules in an open lattice, so ice is less dense than liquid water and floats. Most substances are denser as solids, which makes water unusual.

questions.stem: Why is it important for life in lakes that ice forms on the surface rather than at the bottom?
options: The floating ice insulates the water below, so it stays liquid and organisms survive
The floating ice sinks in spring and stirs nutrients up from the lake bed
The floating ice warms the water below by releasing heat from the Sun
The floating ice keeps oxygen out, so harmful bacteria cannot survive
questions.explanation: Because ice is less dense, it forms a floating layer that insulates the water beneath and slows further freezing. Lakes therefore rarely freeze solid, and organisms survive in the liquid water below.

questions.stem: Water has a much higher boiling point than other molecules of similar size, such as methane. Why does this matter for Earth's systems?
options: Water exists only as ice at Earth's surface, so it forms large ice sheets
Water never evaporates at Earth's surface, so the oceans never lose water
Water stays liquid over the range of temperatures found at Earth's surface
Water boils at room temperature, so it moves easily into the atmosphere
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonding between water molecules raises water's boiling point far above that of similar small molecules, so liquid water is stable across most surface temperatures. This allows oceans, rivers and the water cycle to exist. Water still evaporates below its boiling point.

questions.stem: Water molecules at the surface of a leaf cling together, and water rises through narrow spaces in soil. Which property of water does this mainly show?
options: Low boiling point compared with other molecules
High surface tension and cohesion between water molecules
Low density of water in its solid phase compared with its liquid
Ability to dissolve salts and other ionic substances
questions.explanation: Hydrogen bonds make water molecules attract one another (cohesion), giving water a high surface tension. This helps water form droplets, move through tiny pores in soil and be pulled up through plants during evapotranspiration.

questions.stem: Why is seawater salty?
options: Salt forms when seawater freezes and the ice then melts again each summer
Water dissolves salts weathered from rocks, and rivers carry them to the sea
Salt is produced inside the bodies of marine animals and released into the water
Salt falls into the ocean from the atmosphere as part of every rain shower
questions.explanation: Water is an excellent solvent, so it dissolves ions from rocks during weathering. Rivers carry these ions to the sea, and when seawater evaporates the water leaves but the salts remain, so they build up.

questions.stem: During evapotranspiration from a rainforest, a large amount of energy is absorbed from the surroundings. Which property of water explains this?
options: Water needs a large amount of energy to change from liquid to vapour
Water releases a large amount of energy when it changes to vapour
Water is denser as a vapour than it is as a liquid at the same temperature
Water vapour absorbs no energy, so it rises without changing temperature
questions.explanation: Evaporating water requires a large amount of energy (latent heat), which is absorbed from leaves, soil and air, cooling them. That energy is released again when the vapour condenses in clouds. Water vapour is far less dense than liquid water.

questions.stem: Coastal towns such as Cairns have a smaller range between summer and winter temperatures than inland towns at a similar latitude. Which property of water best explains this?
options: Water absorbs a lot of energy per degree of warming, so it heats and cools slowly
Water reflects nearly all sunlight, so the ocean surface never warms in summer at all
Water boils at a low temperature, so the ocean absorbs heat by boiling in summer
Water is more dense when warm, so warm seawater sinks and cools the coast in summer
questions.explanation: Water has a high specific heat capacity, so the ocean warms and cools much more slowly than land. This moderates the temperature of nearby coasts. Water absorbs most sunlight rather than reflecting it, and warm water is less dense, not more.

questions.stem: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water, mostly in the oceans. Why is this abundance important in Earth system processes?
options: It stops any water from entering the atmosphere, so rainfall comes only from ice sheets
It prevents rocks from being weathered, because the oceans cover the continents
It means fresh water is evenly spread across the land, so droughts cannot occur
It provides a huge store of water and heat that drives the water cycle and moderates climate
questions.explanation: The oceans are the main source of evaporation for precipitation and store and transport vast amounts of heat. Most of Earth's water is salty ocean water, so fresh water on land is limited and unevenly spread.

questions.stem: Over thousands of years, snow that falls on Antarctica each winter does not fully melt in summer. What happens, and which property of water is involved?
options: Snow builds up and compacts into ice sheets, as it stays below freezing there
Snow sinks below the ocean surface, because ice is much denser than seawater
Snow boils away in summer, because water has a very low boiling point
Snow dissolves into the rock beneath, because water dissolves all minerals
questions.explanation: Where temperatures stay below water's freezing point for most of the year, snow builds up faster than it melts, and its weight compacts it into glacial ice, forming ice sheets. Ice is less dense than seawater, so it floats.

questions.stem: Which two sources are proposed for the origin of Earth's water?
options: Chemical weathering of granite and the formation of clouds
Lightning in the atmosphere and the decay of radioisotopes
Volcanic outgassing and impacts of icy bodies from space
Photosynthesis by plants and the melting of polar ice
questions.explanation: Water vapour released from Earth's interior by volcanic outgassing, together with water delivered by water-rich asteroids and comets, is thought to have formed the oceans. Photosynthesis uses water rather than producing the oceans.

questions.stem: The ratio of deuterium (heavy hydrogen) to ordinary hydrogen in Earth's oceans is compared with the ratio in comets and in water-rich meteorites. How is this evidence used?
options: A close match proves that all of Earth's water came from outgassing of the mantle
Any difference proves that no water at all came from space to the early Earth
The ratio shows how old each body is, which tells us when the oceans formed
A close match suggests a body of that type could have been a major source of Earth's water
questions.explanation: Water from different sources carries a characteristic deuterium-to-hydrogen ratio. The ratio in comet 67P measured by the Rosetta mission was about three times that of Earth's oceans, while some water-rich asteroids and meteorites are a closer match. A match is consistent with a source, but does not prove it alone.

questions.stem: Volcanoes today release large amounts of water vapour. How does this support the theory that outgassing contributed to the early hydrosphere?
options: If volcanoes release water now, the more active early Earth probably released much more
It shows volcanoes stopped releasing water once the oceans had fully formed
It proves the oceans formed only in the last few thousand years from eruptions
It shows water vapour comes from the oceans and is recycled through volcanoes only
questions.explanation: Applying uniformitarianism, present-day outgassing suggests the hotter, more volcanically active early Earth released large volumes of water vapour, which condensed as it cooled. Some water in modern eruptions is recycled from subducted plates, but outgassing of original interior water was important early on.

questions.stem: The 'Goldilocks zone' around a star is the range of distances at which:
options: A planet's surface temperature allows liquid water to exist
A planet has enough gravity to hold an atmosphere of oxygen
A planet is close enough for all of its water to be vapour
A planet is far enough away for all of its water to freeze
questions.explanation: In the habitable or Goldilocks zone, a planet is neither too hot nor too cold for liquid water at its surface. This idea is based on models of Earth, where liquid water is essential to Earth system processes and life.

questions.stem: In which layer of the atmosphere does almost all weather occur?
options: The stratosphere
The mesosphere
The thermosphere
The troposphere
questions.explanation: The troposphere is the lowest layer and contains most of the atmosphere's mass and nearly all its water vapour. Air rises and mixes vertically there, forming clouds and weather.

questions.stem: Temperature decreases with height in the troposphere but increases with height in the stratosphere. What causes the increase in the stratosphere?
options: Air in the stratosphere is compressed by the weight of the layers above
Ozone absorbs ultraviolet radiation from the Sun, warming the air
Heat rising from Earth's surface collects at the top of the stratosphere
Clouds in the stratosphere trap infrared radiation from the ground
questions.explanation: The ozone layer within the stratosphere absorbs ultraviolet radiation and converts it to heat, so temperatures rise with height. In the troposphere the air is heated mainly from the ground, so it cools with height.

questions.stem: Why is there little vertical mixing of air in the stratosphere, unlike the troposphere?
options: Cooler air lies above warmer air, so rising air is stopped by strong winds
The stratosphere has no air at all, so there is nothing to move vertically
The stratosphere is full of clouds, which block any air from moving upward
Warmer air lies above cooler air, so the layer is stable and air does not rise
questions.explanation: In the stratosphere temperature increases with height, so warm air sits above cooler air and there is no tendency for air to rise. This stable layering means pollutants injected there, such as volcanic aerosols, can stay for long periods.

questions.stem: Which list gives the layers of the atmosphere in order from Earth's surface upward?
options: Troposphere, mesosphere, stratosphere, thermosphere
Thermosphere, mesosphere, stratosphere, troposphere
Troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere
Stratosphere, troposphere, thermosphere, mesosphere
questions.explanation: From the ground up, the layers are the troposphere, stratosphere, mesosphere and thermosphere. They are defined by whether temperature falls or rises with height in each layer.

questions.stem: Meteors usually burn up high in the atmosphere, in a layer where temperature falls with height to the coldest values in the atmosphere. Which layer is this?
options: The troposphere
The mesosphere
The stratosphere
The thermosphere
questions.explanation: The mesosphere lies above the stratosphere, and temperature decreases with height through it to the coldest temperatures in the atmosphere at its top. Most meteors burn up there as they collide with the thin air.

questions.stem: Temperatures in the thermosphere can reach hundreds of degrees Celsius, yet the layer would not feel hot to a person. Why?
options: The temperature values are wrong, because the thermosphere is very cold
The air is so thin that few molecules are present to transfer heat
The thermosphere contains no oxygen, so heat cannot be measured there
The thermosphere is cooled by clouds of ice crystals reflecting sunlight
questions.explanation: The thermosphere absorbs high-energy solar radiation, so each molecule moves very fast, giving a high temperature. But the air is so thin that very little heat energy would be transferred to an object. Temperature measures average molecular energy, not total heat.

questions.stem: A weather balloon records temperature falling from 25 °C at the ground to −55 °C at 12 km, then rising to about −8 °C at 45 km. Which interpretation is correct?
options: The tropopause is near 12 km; above it the stratosphere warms because ozone absorbs UV
The stratopause is near 12 km; above it the mesosphere warms because of meteors
The tropopause is near 45 km; below it the troposphere warms because of clouds
The mesopause is near 12 km; above it the thermosphere warms because of aurorae
questions.explanation: Temperature falling with height marks the troposphere, and the turning point near 12 km is the tropopause. The rise above it shows the stratosphere, warmed by ozone absorbing ultraviolet radiation. The mesosphere and thermosphere lie higher still.

questions.stem: Where is the ozone layer found, and what is its main role?
options: In the stratosphere, where it absorbs much of the Sun's ultraviolet radiation
In the troposphere, where it traps infrared radiation and warms the surface
In the mesosphere, where it burns up meteors before they reach the surface
In the thermosphere, where it reflects visible light back out into space
questions.explanation: Most of Earth's ozone is concentrated in the stratosphere, roughly 15 to 35 km above the surface. It absorbs most harmful ultraviolet radiation, protecting living things at the surface.

questions.stem: How does ozone form in the stratosphere?
options: Lightning in thunderstorms creates ozone, which rises from the troposphere every day
Plants release ozone during photosynthesis, which drifts upward from forests
Ultraviolet radiation splits oxygen molecules into atoms, which join other oxygen molecules
Volcanoes release ozone gas, which rises directly into the stratosphere and collects
questions.explanation: Ultraviolet radiation breaks O₂ molecules into single oxygen atoms, and each atom can combine with an O₂ molecule to form ozone (O₃). Ozone formation therefore depends on oxygen already being present in the atmosphere.

questions.stem: Historical records of total ozone over Antarctica show values falling sharply each spring from the late 1970s, while records near the equator changed much less. Which conclusion is supported?
options: Ozone near the equator fell faster, because the Sun is strongest at the equator
Ozone loss varies with location and is most severe over Antarctica in spring
Ozone over the whole Earth fell by the same amount at the same time each year
Ozone over Antarctica increased each spring because of cold stratospheric clouds
questions.explanation: The records show the 'ozone hole': severe springtime ozone loss over Antarctica, much greater than at low latitudes. Very cold polar stratospheric clouds help chlorine from CFCs destroy ozone there each spring.

questions.stem: Global Atmosphere Watch, a World Meteorological Organization programme, has stations such as Cape Grim in Tasmania. What is its main purpose?
options: To count the numbers of migratory birds that fly through each country's airspace
To monitor long-term changes in the atmosphere's composition and predict change
To forecast tomorrow's weather for airports and shipping in each member country
To measure earthquakes and volcanic eruptions on the floors of the world's oceans
questions.explanation: Global Atmosphere Watch coordinates measurements of greenhouse gases, ozone, aerosols and other components to identify and understand changes in the atmosphere, predict future change and advise on mitigating human impacts. Daily forecasting is done by national weather services.

questions.stem: According to current theories, Earth's early atmosphere formed mainly from:
options: Water vapour evaporated from oceans that had already formed on Earth
Gases released by volcanic outgassing as Earth cooled and differentiated
Oxygen released by the forests that covered the first continents
Gases blown away from the Sun and captured by Earth
questions.explanation: As Earth cooled and differentiated, gases such as water vapour, carbon dioxide and nitrogen were released from its interior through volcanic outgassing. Forests appeared billions of years later, after the atmosphere already contained oxygen.

questions.stem: Why did Earth's early atmosphere contain much more carbon dioxide than the modern atmosphere?
options: Carbon dioxide was produced by early animals breathing in the shallow seas
Carbon dioxide formed when oxygen reacted with nitrogen in lightning strikes
Carbon dioxide was released by burning forests across the early continents
Outgassed carbon dioxide had not yet moved into oceans, rocks and living things
questions.explanation: Outgassing released large amounts of carbon dioxide. Over time much of it dissolved in the oceans, was locked into carbonate rocks such as limestone, and was used by photosynthesising organisms. Animals and forests appeared much later.

questions.stem: Nitrogen makes up about 78% of the modern atmosphere. Why did it accumulate to become the main gas?
options: It dissolved in seawater more easily than any other atmospheric gas
It formed from carbon dioxide when the first plants grew on land
It was outgassed and is unreactive, so little was removed from the air
It was produced in large amounts by photosynthesis in the early oceans
questions.explanation: Nitrogen was released by outgassing and, because it is chemically unreactive and does not dissolve readily in water, it stayed in the air while carbon dioxide and water vapour were removed. Photosynthesis produces oxygen, not nitrogen.

questions.stem: Which evidence best supports the idea that the early atmosphere contained almost no free oxygen?
options: Very old rocks are bright red, because their iron was oxidised by the atmosphere
Very old rocks contain coal formed from forests that grew on the early land
Very old rocks hold minerals that oxygen would have destroyed by oxidation
Very old rocks contain abundant fossils of large animals that needed oxygen to live
questions.explanation: Some ancient rocks contain grains of minerals such as pyrite that break down quickly in the presence of oxygen, so they could only have survived under oxygen-poor conditions. Red, oxidised rocks and fossils of large animals appear only after oxygen built up.

questions.stem: Which organisms first significantly modified the composition of Earth's atmosphere by adding oxygen?
options: Flowering plants on the early continents
Corals building reefs in shallow seas
Fungi decomposing organic matter in soil
Photosynthesising cyanobacteria in the oceans
questions.explanation: Cyanobacteria were the first organisms to release oxygen through photosynthesis. Over hundreds of millions of years, their oxygen built up in the oceans and atmosphere. Plants, corals and fungi evolved much later.

questions.stem: Banded iron formations are common in rocks older than about 2 billion years but rare in younger rocks. Which explanation best fits the evidence?
options: Plants on land absorbed all of the iron from rivers, so none reached the ocean floor after that
The oceans froze solid, so dissolved iron could no longer move or settle on the sea floor
Oxygen from photosynthesis reacted with dissolved iron until the iron was used up and oxygen accumulated
Volcanoes stopped releasing iron, so the oceans became oxygen-rich without any change in life
questions.explanation: Oxygen released by cyanobacteria reacted with iron dissolved in the oxygen-poor oceans, forming iron oxide layers. Once most dissolved iron had been removed, oxygen began to build up in the oceans and air, and banded iron formations became rare. The rise in atmospheric oxygen began about 2.4 billion years ago.

questions.stem: Why could the ozone layer only develop after photosynthesis had changed the atmosphere?
options: Ozone forms from nitrogen, which was released by early cyanobacteria
Ozone forms from oxygen molecules, which were scarce until photosynthesis released them
Ozone forms from carbon dioxide, which photosynthesis released in large amounts
Ozone forms from water vapour, which photosynthesising organisms produced
questions.explanation: Ozone (O₃) is made when ultraviolet radiation splits O₂ and the atoms join other O₂ molecules. Without the oxygen released by photosynthesis there was little ozone, and ultraviolet radiation reached the surface unhindered. Photosynthesis consumes carbon dioxide rather than releasing it.

questions.stem: How did the formation of the oceans help reduce the amount of carbon dioxide in the early atmosphere?
options: The oceans froze, trapping carbon dioxide in ice that has never melted since
Carbon dioxide dissolved in seawater and was later deposited as carbonate rocks
The oceans released oxygen, which reacted with carbon dioxide to form nitrogen
The oceans reflected sunlight, which broke carbon dioxide into carbon and oxygen
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide dissolves in water, so once the oceans formed they absorbed large amounts from the air. Dissolved carbon combined with calcium and other ions to form carbonate sediments, locking carbon into the geosphere for very long periods.

questions.stem: Which instrument is used to measure atmospheric pressure at a weather station?
options: Anemometer
Hygrometer
Rain gauge
Barometer
questions.explanation: A barometer measures air pressure, usually in hectopascals (hPa). An anemometer measures wind speed, a hygrometer measures humidity and a rain gauge measures rainfall.

questions.stem: Why are thermometers at weather stations kept in a white, ventilated, louvred box such as a Stevenson screen?
options: To seal them from the outside air so that wind cannot change the readings
To make them easier to read from a distance by observers at the station
To shield them from direct sunlight and rain while letting air flow freely
To keep them warmer than the surrounding air so they read more accurately
questions.explanation: The screen measures the true air temperature by protecting the thermometer from direct sun and precipitation, while the louvres allow air to circulate. A sealed box would heat up and give readings that do not match the outside air.

questions.stem: A student records relative humidity at 7 am and 3 pm for a week. Humidity is always higher at 7 am, even though the amount of water vapour in the air changes little. What best explains this?
options: Plants stop transpiring overnight, so water vapour is added to the air only in the morning
Relative humidity measures rainfall, so it is always highest before the day's showers
Cooler morning air can hold less water vapour, so the same vapour is a larger fraction of the maximum
Warmer afternoon air can hold less water vapour, so humidity rises later in the day
questions.explanation: Relative humidity compares the water vapour present with the maximum the air can hold at that temperature. Cool morning air has a lower maximum, so the same amount of vapour gives a higher relative humidity. As the air warms, the maximum rises and relative humidity falls.
